title: DEEP DIVE — The Night in Florence
blurb: 2011 to 2013. AlexNet, built part by part in Hinton's Toronto lab: a photo as a grid of lights, one stencil and its worked number (a convolution), stencils on stencils, stencils learned from noise, a weir that keeps strong signals strong, too few labels for sixty million knobs (crops, mirrors, and dropout, so no lantern can count on another), two halves that split the work their own way, and five days downhill. Then Florence, 12 October 2012, without its professor: 15.3% against 26.2%, a cliff, then the fair caveats. Two candles go out (speech had gone first; within a year every top team used such nets), one is lit and gets its name, deep learning, a desk lamp at the rim clicks on after thirty-six years, and a prophecy goes on the Wall.

shots.setting: the study's candle shelf, then a craftsman's workshop, 2010–2011, evening: tin stencils cut by hand, a judge's lectern, a leaderboard of lanterns

lines.text: Since about 1999, the belief: to see, a machine needs patterns designed by experts, by hand. Even allowed five guesses a picture, the best program missed more than one in four.
lines.direction: respectful of the craft; the belief stated as a reasonable belief, no irony yet; the date plainly
lines.spoken: Since about nineteen ninety-nine, the belief: to see, a machine needs patterns designed by experts, by hand. Even allowed five guesses a picture, the best program missed more than one in four.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the expert-features candle is set on the shelf; in a craftsman's workshop tin stencils are cut by hand, and even with five guesses a quarter of the ring of pictures goes dark. CHAPTER INDEX TAB (the film's chapter-card device for clue chapters): at the shot's first frame a manila index tab, typed in Special Elite with the chapter title 'DEEP DIVE · The Night in Florence', drops down from the frame's top edge at frame top-left like a file-divider tab, holds for 2.5 seconds over the picture, and slides back up; no new shot, no lamp change. CAMERA: SHELF (low macro; the expert-features candle set in its year's place), then the occluder wipe into the workshop. Opens in the study (candleAmber, the film's home base); the tab rides over the start of the first line. Under it, the two steady hands bring a tall candle into the lamp's pool; on 'belief' (as the narration states the belief and its date aloud) they set it on the candle shelf beneath the board, into its year's place (left of the 2006 warm-up candle; CANDLE PLACEMENT), lettered (paraphrase, small caps, Plex Mono) TO SEE, A MACHINE NEEDS FEATURES DESIGNED BY EXPERTS; its base tag reads 'lit 1999'. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here eleven rings have already burned (1999 to 2010): a ghost sleeve of eleven scored rings (66 px) stands above the stub, the flame live where sleeve meets stub. On 'experts' a sheet of dark paper is drawn across frame by an unseen hand (an in-shot occluder wipe, same lamp, never a dim to black) and we are in a paper-cut workshop: a craftsman's silhouette (generic, no likeness) at a bench under a hanging lamp cuts patterns into small tin plates with snips: little gradient arrows, corner marks, edge combs (the hand-designed features of the age, stylised). Finished stencils hang on hooks along the back wall like tools. He carries a stencil to a tall judge's lectern at frame right; behind it a LEADERBOARD OF LANTERNS: paper lanterns hung on strings, each lantern's height = that year's winning error (lower is better), on a ruled scale. On 'five' a single thumbnail (a husky) is pinned on the lectern with five small paper guess-slips fanned beneath it; one slip is the right answer, so the guess counts (top-5 scoring, shown, not said). On 'best' two lanterns glow: 2010 at 28.2%, 2011 at 25.8%, barely a hand's width apart. On 'four' a little more than a quarter of a ring of thumbnails beside the board goes dark (both years missed more than one in four). Date stamp bottom left. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot.

shots.setting: Toronto, 2011–2012, night: a bedroom with a desktop tower holding two gaming cards

lines.text: In Hinton's Toronto lab, Ilya Sutskever, sure deep nets would keep improving with more data, talked Alex Krizhevsky into trying.
lines.direction: storyteller's pace; 'Hinton's' plain (the ear hears whose lab it is); names clear and unhurried

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a Toronto bedroom at night: Sutskever talks Krizhevsky into trying, two gaming cards spin up in a desktop tower, and the lamp clicks off onto a green LED. Plain cut (same candleAmber lamp). Paper-cut bedroom at night (keep décor minimal and generic, after the CHM's photograph of the home computer; invent nothing): a desk, a desk lamp, a window onto a dark street, and a desktop tower (`desktopTower`, gpus: 2, window panel) on the floor. Krizhevsky is seen only from behind at the desk, typing; no words, no views. Sutskever (slight, close-cropped receding hair, plain dark shirt, intense stillness) stands at his shoulder, then leans in; name cards for both on first appearance. Hinton is NOT placed in any invented geography (the narration's 'the tall man's lab' is his research group; the CHM/NVIDIA label carries the contested room): on 'tall' (as the narration names him by the film's epithet) a pre-roll glow gathers at the upper frame edge, and on 'Krizhevsky' a small, separate inset pool of light opens at the upper frame edge, a round lantern-slide picture-in-picture with its own thin brass rim, in which a tall standing silhouette (hinton, standing at a lectern-height desk, never seated in this era's inset) is seen alone; name card 'Geoffrey Hinton, supervisor' (Toronto is on the date stamp). The inset closes before 'cards'; he never enters the room. After the line, the camera tilts down to the tower's side window: two consumer cards, fans spinning up, a whine in the sound design. Then the desk lamp clicks off and the cut MATCHES the lamp's circle to a single green status LED on the card, glowing in the dark. As the tilt begins (just before the GPU label and well before the LED match) the contested note rises as one short label, BEDROOM (CHM) · LAB (NVIDIA), both sources with equal type weight, and stays up through the match and the hold; the full two-source sentence is in creditsSources. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot.

shots.setting: match cut: the Mark I's 20 × 20 photocell eye (Buffalo, 1958) becomes a 224 × 224 × 3 grid (2012)

lines.text: A photograph is a grid of lights, each light a number. In colour, three numbers: red, green, blue. One small photo: a hundred and fifty thousand numbers.
lines.direction: simple and clear; the first step of the build; 'red, green, blue' set down one at a time; 'a hundred and fifty thousand' plain, letting the size land

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: match cut: the Mark I's 20 × 20 photocell eye subdivides into a modern photograph, a grid of lights, each light a number, in three colour planes. Mood stays candleAmber from the bedroom (the desk lamp has just clicked off; the LED-to-cell dissolve carries the light, and the pixel grid's own glow is the shot's practical, so no tint jump). Teaching machine `perceptronRetina` in close-up: the Mark I's 20 × 20 photocell eye from ch03, its four hundred cells glowing on a horizontal bar, stamped BUFFALO · 1958–60 (the Mark I's contested build date, as in ch03-s04 and ch06-s01). The green LED from the last shot dissolves into one of its cells. Camera pulls back as the grid subdivides and multiplies: 400 cells become a 224 × 224 field that resolves into a small backlit photograph (a husky, one of ImageNet's thousand tiles), then, on 'colour', the photo separates like three sheets of coloured tissue into red, green and blue planes stacked in depth, each pixel a tiny lit square. On 'number' one pixel is picked out by a lens and a typed value appears beside it (e.g. 0.73). Just after the line the three planes slide back together and the equation 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 is set in Plex Mono, held in the music. Date stamp changes from BUFFALO · 1958–60 to TORONTO · 2012. The count (about a hundred and fifty thousand numbers) is carried on screen only. SCRIPT NOTE (review round 1): L0805 now names the colour planes and the count: the planes separate on 'colour', and 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 sets on 'hundred'.

shots.setting: a stitched tapestry of the digit 4, a pierced 3 × 3 tin lantern, and a wall that fills with spots of light

lines.text: Hold a pierced tin stencil over the picture, a light behind it.
lines.direction: slow, demonstrative, like holding up a real object

lines.text: Each of its nine holes weighs the light beneath it. Add them up. Below zero counts as zero.
lines.direction: three distinct steps, a beat between each

lines.text: Over an edge, the sum is nearly four: a bright spot. Now the lovely part: slide the same stencil everywhere. A convolution.
lines.direction: the payoff; 'the sum is nearly four' plainly, the number landing on the bright spot; real delight on 'Now the lovely part'; let the slide fall in rhythm with the stencil's steps; then name the idea plainly, as a gift

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a pierced 3 × 3 tin stencil over a stitched digit: nine holes weigh the light, the sum is inked, below zero goes dark, and the same stencil slides everywhere to fill a wall of bright spots. WORD RULE: the narration calls this object a tin stencil; 'lantern' is reserved film-wide for units (the lantern network), so no label or caption here calls the stencil a lantern (the kit name `stencilLantern` stays internal). Teaching machine `stencilLantern` (kernel 'vertical', the real Sobel-style weights −1 0 1 / −2 0 2 / −1 0 1), staged as a paper theatre: the stitched 14 × 14 tapestry of a handwritten '4' at left, the pierced tin stencil hanging over it, the plaster wall at right where its beam falls, ruled into the 12 × 12 feature map. Pierced holes are positive weights (sized by the weight), dark shutters with a cool rim are negative. On 'pierced' showKernel rises: the nine weights are inked beside the nine holes on the stencil itself (part of the machine, not a caption). On 'weighs' the camera pushes into the stencil; the nine weights glow one by one over the nine threads beneath. On 'Add' a parchment plate inks in the nine products, one per hole, middle column included (its weights are zero, so those three terms are visibly 0). On 'zero' a shuttered position over the stroke's right edge shows its sum, −4, rectified to 0: the wall cell stays dark. On 'edge' the stencil glides to the stroke's LEFT edge (row 10, column 7, step 127); the parchment plate shows the worked cell with all nine real values in row order (window rows 0.12 0.24 1 / 0 0.12 1 / 0 0.12 1, verified against DIGIT4 and convolve() in stencilLantern.ts): max(0, (−1)(0.12) + (0)(0.24) + (1)(1) + (−2)(0) + (0)(0.12) + (2)(1) + (−1)(0) + (0)(0.12) + (1)(1)) = 3.88; the beam flares and the brightest spot on the wall lights. On 'Slide' the stencil returns to step 0 and steps in raster order, on twos, accelerating, each wall cell lighting with its real rectified dot product until the full feature map glows: a bright vertical bar wherever a stroke's left edge is. On 'convolution' the camera eases back: the one stencil's shadow is seen repeated, faintly, at every position across the wall (the same nine weights everywhere). Hold on the finished wall in the music. An ILLUSTRATIVE tag sits small at frame bottom from 'pierced' on: this hand-set 3 × 3 stencil on a 14 × 14 digit is a teaching toy; AlexNet's real first-layer stencils are 96 learned 11 × 11 colour stencils (ch08-s05/s06). The general formula spot = max(0, Σ wᵢ · xᵢ) moves to the end-credits sources card; the narration says it in words. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The kernel's numbers live on the stencil; the −4 → 0 shows only as the wall cell's own value.

shots.setting: a cathedral of stencils rising block by block from a rose window that is the photograph

lines.text: Ninety-six stencils at the bottom; four more layers above, each stencilling the one below: edges, then textures, parts, things.
lines.direction: building, stacking; 'each one stencilling the bright spots of the layer below' is the key idea, said clearly; then a gentle crescendo through the four nouns

lines.text: Then two great halls, where every lantern sees everything, and a last hall of a thousand lanterns, one per answer.
lines.direction: the cathedral's top, unhurried; 'one per answer' lands softly

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a cathedral of stencils rises from the photograph's rose window, five courses of detectors built from detectors, then two great halls and a last hall of a thousand lanterns. Teaching machine `alexnetCathedral` (labels on). The husky photograph from s03 becomes the ROSE WINDOW at the base of a two-tower cathedral façade against a dawnGold sky. On 'ninety-six' the first course of stone rises: the conv1 blocks with face width 55 (true shape), and on the rose window's tracery 96 tiny 11 × 11 tiles flicker in (the first-layer stencils). On 'four' the second course rises at face width 27, then three courses at 13, 13, 13 (reveal driven block by block). Between courses, as each course face narrows (55 to 27, 27 to 13), a tiny wordless 3 × 3 window passes over the lower course's bright spots and keeps only the brightest cell of each window (overlapping max-pooling, 3 × 3, stride 2: a diagram mark, no caption), so the eye sees why the picture shrinks, each block's windows lighting as the flow climbs; on 'stencilling' the bright spots of one course are seen feeding up as the picture the next course's stencils slide over (detectors built from detectors). The layer vignettes appear ONE AT A TIME, in the rose-window position itself (never as simultaneous insets): as each course lights, the rose window briefly shows what such a layer responds to, then returns to the photograph: on 'edges' oriented strokes; on 'textures' woven textures; on 'parts' a fur patch and an eye; on 'things' a whole dog's head. On 'halls' TWO great halls rise above the five courses (fc6 and fc7, 4,096 lanterns each; in each, threads fan from every lantern to every lantern below, 'every lantern sees everything'), and on 'last' a third, last hall rises above them that IS a band of a thousand small lanterns, one per category, each with a tiny category tag (fc8, the output; nothing stacks above it; WORD RULE: 'door' is reserved for the chat box in ch12, so this band is never drawn as doors), as the camera pulls back to see the whole cathedral. (Five stencil courses plus three fully connected stages, two great halls and the hall of a thousand lanterns: the paper's five convolutional and three fully connected layers. 'The great halls' in ch08-s08b means exactly the two big halls, fc6 and fc7.) Breaths are opened in the narration after 'edges', 'textures' and 'parts' so each vignette reads (about a second each), not a flicker. Then hold in the music (about 2.5 s) while flow light climbs from window to crown, course by course: as the light reaches each course the rose window replays that course's vignette, one per course (strokes, textures, fur and eye, the dog's head), and settles back to the photograph as the crown lights. No new stair geometry anywhere. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The paper's 'depth really is important' line moves to the end-credits sources card. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots; staging.kitWork): `alexnetCathedral` needs the rose-window layer vignettes (oriented strokes, woven textures, fur patch and eye, dog's head) as a built-in layer, shared with ch08-s06 and ch08-s09.

shots.setting: the cathedral's bridges and columns; noise tiles resolving into a mosaic of 96 learned stencils

lines.text: Nobody cut these stencils. They began as noise, like television snow.
lines.direction: the teacher's own delight; slow, warm, a small smile on 'snow'

lines.text: The messenger from 1986 cut them, nudge by nudge.
lines.direction: a smile of recognition; an old friend returns
lines.spoken: The messenger from nineteen eighty-six cut them, nudge by nudge.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: 96 tiles of television snow are nudged, pass after pass, into the learned mosaic by the 1986 bead. CAMERA: the cathedral's rose window (teaching machine) only; no board insert. Close on the rose window's 96 tiles: they are pure static, grey random speckle. On 'messenger' the dark bead in a ring of light from ch05 (the `lanternNetwork` backward pulse, same design) appears at the cathedral's crown and runs DOWN the cathedral's existing paths only (the column shafts and the bridges between the towers already in `alexnetCathedral`; no new stair geometry), past every course, to the rose window; as it passes each block it tugs its stencils a hair. On 'nudge' the cycle repeats faster and faster (picture after picture: tiny thumbnails flick through the rose window); with each pass the static tiles sharpen until they resolve into the real first-layer mosaic: striped grey edges at every angle and soft colour blobs. On 'mosaic' the last pass lands and the bead fades at the window: the finished mosaic of 96 learned tiles holds, still and uncluttered, through the music-only hold (about 3 s), the chapter's thesis image. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The Florence slide's 'initialized at white Gaussian noise' line moves to the end-credits sources card; the narration already says it. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots; staging.kitWork): `alexnetCathedral` needs a 96-tile filter mosaic with a noise-to-learned morph (t from 0 to 1). If the real AlexNet conv1 weights are not used for the learned state, the mosaic carries a small ILLUSTRATIVE stamp at its lower edge (a stamp, not one of the two text items).

shots.setting: a parchment plate: a weir across a stream, and two paper boats racing

lines.text: Older nets squashed strong signals flat. The below-zero rule is a weir: strong signals pass undimmed, so the messenger's tug stays strong. The net learned six times faster, in the team's test.
lines.direction: crisp, a demonstrator's pleasure; 'squashed ... flat' sets up the contrast; the weir points back to the stencil shot's 'below zero counts as zero'; 'the messenger's tug' a nod to the fading whisper; 'in the team's test' plainly, it is a caveat

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a weir across a stream: the S-curve squashes a tall wave flat, the weir lets it pass at full height, and the rectifier's paper boat wins the race. Parchment plate under its own dawnGold plate lamp (not in the study), drawn in ink and cut paper. LEFT: a stream crossing a small weir; it is the same below-zero rule from the lantern shot, now named as a picture. Water levels arriving from the left are signed numbers; everything below the lip (negative) stops dead, everything above flows over unchanged: the rectifier, f(x) = max(0, x), plotted faintly beneath as its kinked line. On 'squashed' a faint ghost curve of the older S-shaped switch (tanh) inks in beside it and flattens a tall wave against its ceiling; on 'undimmed' the same tall wave passes the weir at full height (ReLU does not saturate for large positive inputs); on 'tug' the backward bead from ch05 runs back across the weir and its ring of light stays bright, where across the S-curve it would have faded. On 'six' a small race: two paper boats, the rectifier's crossing a finish mark well before the old switch's (in their four-layer test on small pictures, not AlexNet itself). Its one label (the rectifier and its measured speed-up) sets in with the weir and is read under the rest of the line. (Max-pooling is not narrated; it is shown wordlessly between the cathedral's courses in ch08-s05.) TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The Florence slide's 'Very good (quick to train)' moves to the end-credits sources card. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots; staging.kitWork): symbolic prop weir.

shots.setting: a balance scale; a hall of shifted mirrors

lines.text: Sixty million weights, yet each label, one name in a thousand, is worth about ten yes-or-no answers. Twelve million answers in all. It could memorise the photos, not learn to see.
lines.direction: the problem, stated plainly; 'one name in a thousand, is worth about ten yes-or-no answers' is the small step the ear needs, said simply; let 'Twelve million answers in all' sit against 'sixty million'; 'memorise' lands as the danger

lines.text: So they cropped and mirrored the pictures.
lines.direction: the first remedy, brisk

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a balance scale: twelve million yes-or-no answers on one pan, sixty million knobs slamming down the other; then a hall of shifted, mirrored crops lifts the answers' side. A paper balance scale. On the left pan, a few small lit tokens, each stamped '≈ 10 bits' (one of 1,000 labels, log₂ 1000 ≈ 10, drawn as ten tiny yes/no toggles); on the right pan, a mountain of tiny knobs (sixty million numbers). On 'twelve' the left pan's tokens are counted into a stack, 1.2 million labels × ≈ 10 = ≈ 12 million answers. On 'Sixty' (the line's first word) the knob mountain lands on the right pan and the scale slams down on the knobs' side; on 'label' the label tokens gather on the left pan, and one token's ten toggles light in turn as the narration says 'about ten yes-or-no answers'. On 'memorise' a single training photograph is pressed flat into the knob mountain like a leaf in a book: the danger of learning the pictures by heart; on 'see' a faint ghost of a learned edge-stencil tile beside it stays unlit (what it should have learned instead). On 'cropped' the camera passes into a hall of mirrors: one photograph (the husky) reflected into many slightly shifted 224-pixel crops of the 256-pixel image, and on 'mirrored' each one flipped left-right in a second mirror; counter: × 2048. Their light pours onto the left pan, which rises (but not all the way). Dropout is its own shot next. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The paper's '10 bits of constraint' sentence moves to the end-credits sources card; the narration ('about ten yes-or-no answers', 'twelve million in all') and the label carry it. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots; staging.kitWork): symbolic prop balanceScale.

shots.setting: the cathedral's two great halls in miniature: a loom of lanterns, a different random half snuffed on every example

lines.text: In the great halls, they snuffed a random half each time, so no lantern could count on another. Like a team where anyone might be missing, each had to know the work.
lines.direction: slow and clear; let 'each time' be heard; 'count on another' is the reason, said simply; then the team picture warmly and plainly, as if it were obvious once seen; the music then takes over

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the two great halls in miniature: on every example a different random half of the lanterns is snuffed, so no lantern can lean on another. Plain cut. Teaching machine `lanternNetwork`, drawn as the cathedral's great halls in miniature: below, a short stub of the stencil courses, fully lit and never snuffed; above, the two big fully connected halls as a wide loom of lanterns (fc6 and fc7), then the last hall of a thousand lanterns (fc8, never snuffed). KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots; listed in staging.kitWork, and built with a gallery entry before this shot is authored): extend `lanternNetwork` with {mask, maskSeed, topology: custom layer sizes + fixed weights} (p = 0.5, a fresh seed per example) so the snuffing is bound to real data, per the bible's §6 recipe. On 'halls' the camera rises to the two halls. On 'snuffed' a thumbnail slides into the base, and exactly the lanterns the mask zeroes in fc6 and fc7 go dark, each with a wisp of smoke; light flows up only through the survivors. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Three candles matter here. The expert-features candle (TO SEE, A MACHINE NEEDS FEATURES DESIGNED BY EXPERTS, tag 'lit 1999'): on 'thirteen' it gutters and goes out with thirteen rings burned (1999 to 2012), a dark ghost sleeve of thirteen scored rings (78 px) above its stub, a thread of smoke rising; its tag is re-inked '1999 – 2012 · 13'.
